The length of a journal can serve as a data point that can help understand the extent of participants’ self-disclosure and expression. First, a correlation analysis was conducted to determine how the number of LLM feature requests (i.e., Generating sentences using keywords, Recommending next sentences) affected the participants’ journal length. In the case of Recommending next sentences, there was a moderately positive correlation with the length of the journal (𝑟 = .5797, 𝑝 = .003), but in the case of Generating sentences using keywords, there was no significant correlation (𝑟 = −.2479, 𝑝 = .242). We wondered if the journal was getting long simply because the participants used LLM-generated sentences. Therefore, we further investigated whether there was a correlation between the number of sentences participants selected (brought) from the LLM’s suggestions and journal length. Interestingly, there was no significant correlation between journal length and the number of sentences chosen to use from the LLM suggestions (Generating sentences using keywords: r = -.2253, 𝑝 = .2898, Recommending next sentences: 𝑟 = .1886, 𝑝 = .3775) (See Figure 4). In summary, these results imply that the more users browse the LLM-generated sentences from Recommending the next sentences, the more likely they will write. However, the number of sentences participants incorporated into their journals was not correlated with the journal length. In other words, the increased length of the journal wasn’t merely due to the convenience of having text written on their behalf.

reaction_window_summary.baseline_explanation:
This passage marks a transition in the authors' analysis. After examining *when* and *how frequently* participants used the AI features, the researchers shift their focus to investigating the *specific content and nature* of the AI-generated sentences that users actually chose to incorporate into their private journals. 

To do this, they highlight a key interaction design choice of their system, DiaryMate: rather than automatically inserting text, the system generates up to five distinct sentence suggestions upon request, allowing the user to select the one that best fits their thoughts. 

This design choice is highly relevant to the paper's core theme of human-AI collaboration. By offering a menu of options, the system preserves the user's agency and control over their deeply personal narrative. The user acts as a curator or editor, which is crucial in a reflective task like journaling where authenticity and self-ownership are paramount. 

Ultimately, analyzing these selected sentences allows the researchers to evaluate how effectively the LLM aids in self-disclosure and emotional reflection, while also helping them identify potential risks, such as users over-relying on AI-generated expressions to articulate their own feelings.

reaction_window_summary.baseline_explanation:
This passage introduces the researchers' investigation into the specific content and characteristics of the AI-generated sentences that users chose to adopt into their personal diaries. 

In the context of the paper, the "DiaryMate" system supports users by offering two generative features: generating sentences from user-provided keywords and recommending the next sentence in a sequence. For each request, the system presents up to five options, giving the user control over which sentence (if any) best fits their narrative. Having established *when* and *how often* users interacted with these features, the authors transition here to analyzing the qualitative nature of the selected sentences.

This analysis is crucial because it helps reveal the role the LLM plays in highly personal, reflective writing. By looking at the types of sentences users accepted, the researchers can understand whether participants used the AI for emotional articulation, structural assistance, or creative inspiration. Ultimately, this informs how future human-AI collaborative tools can support self-expression without overshadowing the user's authentic voice.

title: DiaryMate: Understanding User Perceptions and Experience in Human-AI Collaboration for Personal Journaling
one_sentence_summary: This study examines how users interact with an LLM-based journaling assistant to understand the balance between user intent and AI involvement in personal, introspective writing.
research_problem: A gap in understanding people's perceptions and experiences with Large Language Models (LLMs) in the specific context of personal and retrospective writing tasks.
method_summary: The researchers developed DiaryMate as a technology probe and conducted a 10-day field study followed by interviews to observe real-world usage and perceptions.
dataset_or_materials: The DiaryMate system (featuring keyword-based and next-sentence generation) and data from a field study involving 24 participants (N=24).
main_findings: Participants utilized LLM-generated sentences to reflect on past experiences from multiple perspectives, yet showed signs of over-reliance by prioritizing AI-generated emotional expressions over their own.
key_terms: human-centered computing, empirical studies in hci, journaling,
